claims.text: Git combines the two sides region by region against the commit they share — a region being a run of neighbouring lines: where only one side changed a region it takes that change without asking, and it stops only where both sides changed the same region.
claims.source_hint: git-merge documentation, 'HOW CONFLICTS ARE PRESENTED' (non-overlapping changes to an area taken verbatim; both sides changing the same area asks you to resolve)

claims.text: When a merge stops at a conflict Git records the path as unmerged, leaves the markers in the working tree and writes no commit; the branch still points where it did before the command.
claims.source_hint: git-merge documentation, 'HOW CONFLICTS ARE PRESENTED' and 'TRUE MERGE'; git-status documentation on unmerged paths

claims.text: In `git status --short`, a path both sides modified is printed with the two-letter code `UU`; `--branch` adds a leading line of the form `## <branch>`.
claims.source_hint: git-status documentation, 'Short Format' (the unmerged status letters table and -b/--branch)

claims.text: Git fences a conflicted region with `<<<<<<<` plus the current side's label, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` plus the other side's label; in a merge the first section, opened by `<<<<<<<`, is the branch you are on. With `diff3` a `|||||||` section holding the shared version sits directly above `=======`.
claims.source_hint: git-merge documentation, 'HOW CONFLICTS ARE PRESENTED' (the marker example)

claims.text: With `merge.conflictStyle` set to `diff3`, Git writes a third section into the fenced region, opened by `|||||||` and holding the text from the commit both sides share; the default style writes only the two sides.
claims.source_hint: git-config documentation, merge.conflictStyle (default 'merge', values 'diff3'/'zdiff3'); git-merge documentation, 'HOW CONFLICTS ARE PRESENTED'

claims.text: `git -c <name>=<value> <command>` applies that configuration value to the one command only.
claims.source_hint: git documentation (git(1)), -c <name>=<value>

claims.text: `git add <path>` on a conflicted path stages the file's current content as the resolution, whatever that content is, and clears its unmerged state; nothing in the documented merge flow compares what you staged against either side afterwards.
claims.source_hint: git-add documentation, DESCRIPTION (adding a conflicted path marks it resolved); git-merge documentation, 'HOW TO RESOLVE CONFLICTS'

claims.text: After the conflicted paths are added, `git commit` concludes a merge and `git rebase --continue` concludes a rebase.
claims.source_hint: git-merge documentation, 'HOW TO RESOLVE CONFLICTS'; git-rebase documentation, --continue

claims.text: `git merge --abort` and `git rebase --abort` try to reconstruct the state from before the command and keep nothing of it; if you had uncommitted changes when the command started, Git may be unable to restore them, which is why the documentation says to commit or stash first.
claims.source_hint: git-merge documentation, --abort; git-rebase documentation, --abort

claims.text: A rebase applies the replayed commits one at a time, so it can stop at a conflict once per replayed commit, whereas a merge stops at most once.
claims.source_hint: git-rebase documentation, DESCRIPTION (commits reapplied one by one, stopping on failure) and --continue

claims.text: During a rebase the sides are named from the replay's point of view: 'ours' is the work already in place that the commits are being replayed onto, and 'theirs' is the commit being replayed — the reverse of the merge case.
claims.source_hint: git-rebase documentation, NOTES on ours/theirs being swapped during rebase; git-checkout documentation, --ours/--theirs

claims.text: `git merge` reports failure when it stops at a conflict: the captured run prints `Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.` The script `scripts/git/conflict-demo.sh` runs under `set -euo pipefail` (line 3) and appends `|| true` to the merge line (line 11).
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: scripts/git/conflict-demo.sh lines 3, 11; outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/conflict-demo.txt line 3; git-merge documentation, DESCRIPTION (no EXIT STATUS section)

claims.text: The captured run of scripts/git/conflict-demo.sh at stage-0 prints `Auto-merging total.sh`, `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in total.sh` and `Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.`, then `UU total.sh`.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/conflict-demo.txt lines 1-6

claims.text: Resolving by taking one whole side replaces every region of the file with that side's text, including the regions Git already merged without conflict; only the fenced region was in dispute.
claims.source_hint: git-checkout documentation, --ours/--theirs (checks out the file's version from that stage, whole file); git-merge documentation, 'HOW CONFLICTS ARE PRESENTED'

claims.text: Opinion: the longer a branch runs alone the more regions it changes, so the more regions it can collide in, and a branch that lands in a day tends to keep conflicts small. A tendency, not a rule: a long-lived branch touching files nobody else touched conflicts nowhere.
claims.source_hint: outline item 4 of foundation.l2.git-conflicts; follows from claim 1 (conflicts are per changed region)

claims.text: Opinion: a conflict is not evidence of a mistake; it is what two deliberate changes to the same lines look like, and the resolution that keeps both sides' intent is usually the correct one — as here, where the invoice needs both the rounding and the unit.
claims.source_hint: outline misconception 1 of foundation.l2.git-conflicts; examples/don-hang at stage-0: the two commits changing total.sh

claims.text: `git switch --quiet -c <name> <start-point>` creates and checks out a branch at that start point without the usual message, and `--no-edit` on `git merge` accepts the generated message without opening an editor; neither changes how a conflict is detected or presented.
claims.source_hint: git-switch documentation, -c/--create, --quiet and <start-point>; git-merge documentation, --no-edit

claims.text: `--abort` aborts the conflict resolution process that is currently in progress, so it is available only while the command is stopped; once the merge is committed there is no merge in progress and nothing left to abort.
claims.source_hint: git-merge documentation, --abort ('Abort the current conflict resolution process') and 'HOW TO RESOLVE CONFLICTS' (--continue checks for a merge in progress); git-rebase, --abort
